newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore ministers sue opposition politician.
newsitem.headline: Singapore ministers sue opposition politician.

text.p: Singapore Deputy Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong and Education Minister Lee Yock Suan are suing an opposition politician for libel over statements they say he made in the recent election campaign, a lawyer said on Thursday.

Tan Kok Quan, a partner in law firm Lee & Lee, which is acting for the deputy prime minister, told Reuters his practice had served notice of the action on Tang Liang Hong through an advertisement on Wednesday in the daily Straits Times newspaper.

Tang, a defeated Workers' Party candidate in a hotly contested constituency at the January 2 polls, is currently out of Singapore. He left Singapore shortly after the elections, saying he had received death threats.

Tang was criticised repeatedly during the election campaign by Prime Minister Goh Chok Tong and other members of the ruling People's Action Party as an extremist with views they said could threaten the harmony of multi-racial Singapore.
Among other charges, Goh said Tang had told a seminar that Chinese-educated Singaporeans "were carrying the sedan chair for others" when they "should be sitting in the sedan chair".
Race is a sensitive issue in Singapore, which suffered brief but bloody race riots in the 1960s between the majority ethnic Chinese and minority Malay communities.
Tan said the newspaper advertisement "was a substituted service because (notice) couldn't be served on Tang Liang Hong personally".
Tang told Reuters by mobile phone that he would contest all the claims made by the Singapore ministers in their suits. He said he was speaking from London.

The Lee & Lee advertisement said Lee Hsien Loong, son of former Singapore prime minister Lee Kuan Yew, was claiming damages for libel in a report Tang lodged with police during the campaign and re-published in various newspapers.

Tang told Reuters his report to the police referred to statements made by 11 members of the Singapore government, including the two ministers acting against him, alleging he was anti-Christian and a "Chinese Chauvinist". Tang had said in the report that the allegations were groundless and intended to harm his reputation.
The Lee & Lee advertisement said the deputy prime minister was seeking an unspecified amount for damages and legal costs.
Tang had eight days to answer the charges, it said.
A similar advertisement, placed on behalf of Lee Yock Suan, said judgement could be entered against Tang if he did not answer the charges within the eight day period.
Tang told Reuters he was not anti-Christian or a racist and said the legal moves against him were politically motivated.
"They want to bury me with a series of actions," he said.
He said he would answer all the charges within the eight days and would eventually return to Singapore.
Prime Minister Goh and and Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew had earlier said they would sue Tang for defamation over different statements made during the campaign.
The ruling People's Action Party halved the opposition presence in the 83-member parliament from four seats to two in the election.
